Stress-Testing the Whole Budget

Lenders stress-test your mortgage against a higher rate. Almost nobody stress-tests the rest of their borrowing at the same time.

Your mortgage lender stress-tests your mortgage. Nobody stress-tests the rest of your borrowing, and nobody adds the two together. That gap is where household financial trouble usually starts.

What the lender does, and what it leaves out

A mortgage lender checks you could still afford the payment if rates were higher than the rate you're actually being offered. It's a real test, and it protects you as well as them.

But it only tests one debt against one shock. It assumes your income holds, your other commitments stay as declared, and nothing else happens. Real financial difficulty rarely arrives that tidily. It usually turns up as two things at once: the rate rises and the hours get cut; the fix ends and the car needs replacing.

Running the test properly

If you do this once, on paper, and keep it, it takes about twenty minutes.

Step one: the current picture

List every monthly commitment: mortgage or rent, every loan, every card minimum, car finance, insurance, council tax, energy, water, phone, essential subscriptions, food, transport. Total it, and compare it against your take-home pay. The difference is your actual monthly margin, the number that decides whether a shock is an inconvenience or a crisis.

Step two: the rate shock

Take every variable or soon-to-expire debt and re-price it two or three percentage points higher.

  • Mortgage: payment change forecaster. If your fix ends within two years, use the higher rate, not today's.
  • Everything variable: rate stress test, one debt at a time.

Add up the new payments, and subtract them from your income. Is the margin still positive?

Step three: the income shock

Now, separately, hold rates where they are, and cut household income by a third instead — one earner losing hours, a bonus not arriving, a period of illness. Ask the same question again.

Step four: both at once

This is the one that matters, and it's the one nobody runs. Higher rates and lower income, together. If your margin's still positive here, you're genuinely robust. If it isn't — and for a lot of households it isn't — you've found something useful, early, while there are still cheap options open to you.

Do this before you borrow more, not after. Before, every option's open: borrow less, keep the term short, clear a debt first, wait. After, your options are the expensive ones. The test costs twenty minutes, and it may be the most useful twenty minutes you spend on your finances.

What to do when the answer is uncomfortable

Roughly in order of effect:

  1. Build the emergency fund first. Three to six months of essential outgoings, in an instant-access account. This is what turns a shock into an inconvenience, and no clever debt structuring substitutes for it.
  2. Kill the highest-payment-to-balance debts. Those are the ones consuming the most monthly margin per pound owed. Clearing them buys back margin fastest, and, as it happens, buys back mortgage borrowing power too.
  3. Fix what you can't afford to have move. If the mortgage rising would break the budget, certainty is worth paying for.
  4. Borrow less than the maximum. The lender's maximum is a constraint, not a recommendation. Nobody has ever regretted a mortgage that was comfortably affordable.
  5. Keep the term short where you can. A longer term means a lower payment and a higher total cost. If a long term is the only way the sums work, that's information in itself about whether the purchase is the right size.

Redo it when something changes

The test goes out of date. Re-run it when your fix is within a year of ending, when you take on any new commitment, when your income changes shape, and once a year regardless. It's much quicker the second time.

And if the honest answer today is that your margin's already negative, or close to it, don't wait for the stress test to become real. There are free services who will help, and every one of them will tell you the same thing: the options are much better before arrears than after.
